translations.text: Ptolemy Philometor learned from those who had returned to him that Antiochus had occupied the territories he ruled and taken them from him. He ordered all his forces, both cavalry and infantry, to arm themselves. He also took his sister Arsinoe with him and came to the region of Raphia, where Antiochus's army was encamped.

A man named Theodotus, wishing to carry out his plot, devised a plan and took with him armed, powerful men from Ptolemy's forces who had previously pledged themselves to him. He came by night and attacked Ptolemy's tent to kill him alone and so bring the [?] to an end.

Dositheus son of Drimylus learned of this. He was called a Jew and had later accepted the law, but he was a stranger to the covenant of the ancestors. He put a poor man in Ptolemy's tent, and that man happened to be killed in place of the king.

The battle was fierce, and matters were going very well for Antiochus. Arsinoe went among the troops with her hair loose, weeping with many tears and sobs. She begged them to save themselves, their wives, and their children, and to fight bravely. She promised to give each man two minas of gold if they fought and won.
And so it happened: all their opponents fell before them, and they captured many of them wounded.
After Ptolemy had won, he decided to go up to the nearby cities and rebuild them.
He did so, granted exemptions to the temples of their religion, gave them gifts, and strengthened them and established them under his authority.

The Jews also sent some of the elders and senior men of the people to Philometor to exchange greetings and bring him a gift and expressions of joy at his victory. When he received these from them, he was delighted and became even more eager to visit them.
He came to Jerusalem and offered sacrifices to the great and mighty God. He also honored the place with many offerings.
When he saw the construction of the place, its orderly arrangement, and the splendor of the temple, he decided to enter the temple's interior as well.

They told him, "You are not permitted to do this, because neither the members of our people nor even all the priests are permitted to enter, but only the high priest, once a year." But none of this persuaded him.
They brought the law and read it before him, but he still would not be persuaded. Instead, he said, "I must enter. Even if they have been deprived of this honor, I will not be deprived of it."
He questioned them, saying, "Why is it that when I enter all the temples of religion, none of those inside them has stopped me?"
One of them answered him confidently, "You are wickedly [?] this."
But he answered, "Whether you wish it or not, I must enter."

The priests put on their sacred garments and fell on their faces. They cried out and pleaded before the great and mighty God to help and deliver them and to turn aside his evil intention and wicked plan. They filled the temple with tears and the sound of crying.
All the city's inhabitants were trembling and alarmed. They rushed out, waiting to see what would happen.
The young women who had been kept secluded came out with their mothers, with dust and ashes strewn on their heads. They wandered through the streets with weeping, tears, and sobs.
Brides who had only just married left their bridal chambers for the occasion and the covering of their modest attire, and ran about bewildered in the street without shame.
Women left their infants and wandered here and there through the streets and open places. All the people gathered and came to the glorious temple.
They cried out and pleaded that his intention and everything he had planned might be thwarted.
When the people saw that he was insisting on entering and could not be persuaded to abandon his evil intention,

they said to one another in a loud voice that they should take up their weapons and be ready to die bravely for the law and the covenants of their ancestors. There was great turmoil and commotion in the place. With difficulty, some of the priests and elders stood up, forcibly restrained the people, and turned them to prayer and cries for help.
All the people stood before them in prayer and supplication.
The officials and honored men who were with the king tried every means, begging and urging him to turn back and abandon his evil intention and wicked plan.
But he was not persuaded by any of these things. Instead, he grew proud and arrogant and began to enter by force, thinking that he would carry out his intention.

While these things were happening, even those with him saw what was happening and turned back in fear. They saw all the people pleading and calling upon the one who holds authority over everything to turn punishment and disaster against their enemies, and not to overlook the unjust deed and the arrogant, boastful act being committed in violation of the law.
They all gathered together, pleading and crying out with sobbing too great to describe.

The sound was such that it seemed that not only human beings were crying out, but also the walls and foundations, and even the earth itself. All of them were ready to surrender their lives to death for the temple, so that it would not be defiled.
Simon the high priest knelt before the altar, stretched out his hands, and prayed with wisdom, saying:

“Lord, Lord, King of heaven and Master of all, holy Judge among the holy ones, you alone are first, the Almighty. Look upon us, for we are being oppressed by an unclean, defiled, arrogant man, a feeble and wretched power.
For you created everything, and you hold everything by your righteous power. For you act against all those who exalt themselves and grow arrogant in everything.

You judged those of old who committed injustice, and you destroyed even the giants among them, who trusted in the strength of their might, with the overwhelming waters of the flood that could not be restrained.

When the wickedness of the people of Sodom was revealed and became known, you burned them with fire and sulfur, because they were proud and arrogant in their deeds. You made them an astonishing spectacle to all the generations after them.

You tormented and scourged the great and arrogant Pharaoh, who enslaved your holy people Israel, with every kind of plague. You made known the power of your greatness and displayed your mighty dominion.

When he pursued your people with horses, chariots, and a great multitude, you drowned him in the depths of the sea with his entire army. But those who trusted in you, who can do whatever you wish throughout all creation, you kept safe and sound.
And when your servants saw, they praised you, Almighty.

You, the King who made the earth, which cannot be measured or surveyed, chose this city and consecrated this place for your name, though you need nothing. You glorified it by revealing the greatness of your splendor, and gave it a name and a covenant for the praise of your great and honored name.

Because you established and loved the house of Israel, you promised them that if they sinned and turned away from you, and afflictions and troubles overtook them, and they came and prayed in this place, you would hear their pleading.
And now, you are faithful and true.
For many times, when our ancestors were oppressed, you helped them in their afflictions and rescued them from every trouble and every danger.
And now, holy King, because of our great and numerous sins, we are being oppressed and enslaved to our enemies, and we remain in our weakness.
And look, this wicked, unclean, defiled man wishes to dishonor the holy place that was chosen and made known on earth for your excellent and holy name.
For your dwelling is in the highest heaven, exalted above all human beings.
But because you wished your glory to dwell among your people Israel, you consecrated this place.

Therefore, do not punish us through the uncleanness of these people, or discipline us through their defilement, so that the unjust may not boast in their wickedness or rejoice in their arrogant speech and say,
‘We have trampled the sanctuary just as the temples of idols are trampled.’
But wipe away our sins, forgive our offenses, and let your face shine upon us at this hour.
Let your mercy quickly come to meet us, Lord. Put your praise in the mouths of the humble and brokenhearted, and grant us peace

in this place.” Then the Lord God, who sees everything, the Father of fathers and the Holy One of holy ones, heard his prayer and pleading, and struck the man who a little earlier had been boasting and exalting himself,

on this side and that, and tormented him with great distress. He collapsed and fell to the ground, trembling all over like a reed before the wind, so that he could not even speak a word because of the punishment of the righteous judgment that had confronted him.
When his friends and guards saw the severe punishment that had overtaken him, they feared that he might even die. Immediately they dragged him outside, filled with great fear.
After a little while, he revived and came to his senses, but he would not turn away from his stubborn resolve. Instead, threatening them in great and fierce anger, he left that place.
When Philometor went to Egypt, his wickedness continued to grow and increase, together with that of all his nobles and friends, who were devoid of all righteousness.

Their many, countless [?] were not enough for him. He went so far in his insolence as to speak blasphemous words against the place. Many of his friends, seeing the king's attitude, also agreed with the wicked man's intentions.
The king issued a written decree against the members of our people. He also made a carved image and set it up between the towers of the courtyard.

He wrote that anyone who did not sacrifice to it was not to enter the temple of God. All Jews were to be registered and brought into service and subjection as slaves. Those among them who resisted were to be brought by force and tortured to death.
Those who were registered were to be branded with fire with the mark of Dionysus, so that they would be under the king's subjection.

So that it would not appear to many that “we are compelling them by force,” he wrote as follows: “All those among them who wish to share the outlook of our religion are to be registered as Alexandrians, citizens of his city—the king's city.”

A few of them, whose resolve was not firm in the worship of God and in the ordinances of our city, readily surrendered themselves. As though they were joining in something good and excellent, they complied with the king's command.

But the majority of the people took courage and stood firm heroically. They did not abandon or depart from any righteousness, but surrendered their possessions for the sake of their lives, to save themselves from registration.

They hoped and waited for deliverance to come to them. Those who separated themselves and departed from them they regarded as unclean and considered enemies, excluding them from the privilege of fellowship in their assemblies.

As soon as the wicked man heard these things, he became exceedingly angry. His rage was directed not only against those living in Alexandria; he also became a bitter opponent of the people living throughout the country. He ordered that they all be gathered together quickly and urgently and put to a cruel and bitter death.
When this command was given, an evil and bitter report about all our people spread through men who had turned away from the law, because they had not allowed them to share fellowship with them.
The Jews, however, maintained their loyalty to the king.
They were careful to observe God's ordinances and laws and maintained the distinctions concerning foods. Because of this, they appeared to many to be arrogant and conceited.
Yet they conducted themselves with righteousness in everything they did and were seen to be chosen and distinguished above all other people.
As for the decree issued against our people that they should be counted among the nations, they were unable to register them by force.

Because they would not submit to their foods and their acts of worship, they spread a report against them that they were saying, “We have no regard for the king, nor will we agree to serve his forces.” They claimed that they were rebellious people who strongly opposed the king's commands and purposes. It was no small matter how they spread their hatred and their malicious report.

The Gentiles living in the city had seen nothing wrong in the Jews who lived among them. They saw the calamity and turmoil that had suddenly come upon them and the hurried course of coercion, but they could do nothing to help them, because the decree against them was harsh and severe. In great distress, they begged and pleaded with their oppressors, saying to them:
“Do not oppress them so cruelly. Surely this whole multitude of people cannot be destroyed when they have done nothing wrong.”

Some of their friends and neighbors also began buying them off and pleading with the oppressors as a ruse, saying to them, “We will make them offer sacrifices.” But the Jews continued in prayer and cries for help, waiting and looking for deliverance to come to them.

The king, however, boasted and exalted himself, growing more defiant in his inflated mind. He paid no attention to the dominion of the great God, but thought he would always remain in this state of mind and in this mighty authority. He wrote and sent them the following letter:
“King Ptolemy Philometor, to the generals, governors, and soldiers of Egypt and every region: greetings and good health.
“I too am well, and our affairs [?].
After we had won the victory and returned from the war we fought in Asia, which you yourselves also know about, with the help of the invincible gods who were with us,
we wished to deal with all the peoples living in Syria and Phoenicia, not through oppression or force, but with great gentleness and mercy, as indeed we did.
We gave many great offerings to all the priests in every city, and we decided to go up to Jerusalem as well and honor the temple of those wretched and perpetually foolish people.
They welcomed our arrival in words, but in their actions they treated us as strangers. For when we wished to enter their temple and honor it with gifts and great honors,
in the arrogance and conceit that possessed them, they prevented us from entering. They deprived themselves of the honor we wished to show them in keeping with our love for everyone.

They disclosed and displayed their hatred toward us, as though we ruled only over the other nations. Because of their arrogance and conceit, they treated their constant benefactors with contempt and showed them no love.
We were deeply distressed by these people's insolence and foolishness, and we returned to Egypt victorious. We welcomed all the peoples with joy and peace, and acted as was proper for us.

We held no grudge or anger against these people or their fellow countrymen, for we were living in harmony and agreement. We entrusted affairs to them and left them in their hands. We forgave the offenses and insolent acts they had committed many times in the past, and we wished to register them as Alexandrians, citizens of our city and associates of the priests of our ancestors.
But they kept looking for and anticipating hostility. With the wickedness rooted in them, they rejected kindness and cast it away from themselves, because they are always intent on evil.

Not only did they refuse to abandon and turn away from their foolish and contemptible religion, but they also despise, in word and deed, the few found among them who are loving and loyal toward us. They constantly oppose us and overturn every decree and law we establish.
They oppose us in everything. Perhaps, if war should break out between us and our enemies, these wicked and wretched people will also join them against us and become our betrayers and enemies.

For this reason, we have issued and sent this command: the moment you receive this letter of ours, arrest those described in it, together with their wives, their children, and everything they possess. Send them to us in disgrace and captivity, bound in iron and subjected to every hardship.
For when these people have been removed from us and destroyed, we will always have peace and tranquility in our kingdom. You will grow in prominence and wealth and draw closer to my favor.
If anyone hides any of the Jews, from the elderly down to children and infants nursing at the breast, he and his entire household shall die in anguish and severe torment.

Whoever comes forward and informs against him shall be given the property of the person found guilty of this offense. He shall also receive three thousand pieces of silver from Caesar's treasury, freedom, and a crown.
Every place where a Jew is found hiding shall be burned with fire and laid waste like a wilderness. The people living there shall be destroyed and wiped out from among humanity.
Such was the wording of the copy of the letter.
Wherever this decree was heard, it brought the nations joy, great exultation, and delight, as though they had been waiting for this to happen and had now been openly authorized to carry it out.

But the Jews mourned greatly. They wept aloud, cried out, and groaned deeply, for pain and sorrow had reached their hearts. Distress surrounded them on every side, and a sentence of destruction and death had suddenly come upon them, which they had not expected.
For what city or inhabited place, what streets or open country, were not filled with mourning and great lamentation?

They were being arrested by the governors in every city with violence and severe, bitter oppression, and were being tortured. Their suffering was so harsh and bitter that when their enemies saw it, they were distressed and wept over them.
For they saw many respected elders being led away in disgrace and with great violence, while their captors felt not the slightest shame before them.

The brides who had just been married left the bridal chambers of their youth and took on mourning instead of joy. Instead of perfumes, they poured ashes over their heads and were brought along by force, stripped of their bridal covering and modesty.
They were bound and shackled in iron by foreigners, driven along under harsh treatment, and brought through the streets to the ships.

Their husbands too were driven along and brought by force. Instead of wedding crowns, iron collars were put around their necks. Instead of the joy and pleasure of youth and the delight of the remaining days of their wedding celebration, they were in mourning, weeping, and sighing, for they saw their death before their eyes.
They were forced down into the ships like animals, bound and shackled in iron. Some were chained by their necks and others by their feet.
Others were bound and fastened to the ships’ planks, so that they would be confined in every possible way on all sides, without even a little relief.

When they had all boarded the ships and come to the king, he ordered them to camp outside the city in an open place, exposed to disgrace and public humiliation, where anyone who wished could go out and look at them. He surrounded and encircled them with a force of his soldiers so that none of them could escape.
After doing this, he heard that some of their own people were going out to them, weeping and sighing over the misery and calamity that had befallen their fellow Jews.
He became furious and exceedingly angry, and ordered that these people too should be subjected to every hardship, just like their companions, with nothing of the others’ suffering spared them.
He also ordered them all to be registered by name, and set a day on which he would destroy and wipe them all out.
They began registering them under harsh and bitter oppression, working with great diligence from sunrise to sunset. He had given them forty days to register them all.

Meanwhile, the king rejoiced and enjoyed himself, holding a great banquet in the temple of his idols, in the blindness and great arrogance that possessed him. With his defiled mouth and foolish mind, he praised the mute, blind idols that neither speak nor hear. He despised and rejected justice and righteousness, and spoke blasphemous words.
After the time assigned to the registrars, they approached the king and said to him, “We are unable to register all the Jews, because there are so very many of them.”
“They cannot be counted, because the country is full of them, and there is no house without some of them in it. It is certain that the governors of Egypt cannot count them.”

When the king heard these things from them, he became exceedingly angry with them, claiming that they had taken bribes from the Jews and had seized on an excuse to say these things about them. Then they came forward and assured him that they were telling the truth.
They showed him the sheets on which they had registered them, and told him that they had also used up and exhausted all their reed pens.
This happened through the working of God’s invincible power to help the Jews.

Then the king summoned Hermon, who had been appointed chief and supervisor of the elephants, and ordered him to take great care of the elephants, for the king was inflamed and filled with uncontrollable fury and anger.

He said to him, “Tomorrow give all the elephants, numbering about five hundred, plenty of frankincense and undiluted wine to drink. Enrage them with a great quantity of intoxicating drink, so that he may bring them in and unleash them on the Jews to destroy and wipe them out.”
After giving these orders, he turned to his pleasures and summoned his friends and officials, those who hated the Jews most intensely.
The supervisor of the elephants, whose name was Arharot, carried out what had been commanded to Hermon.

Every evening their attendants went out and bound the hands of the wretched and destitute prisoners. They kept careful watch over them and guarded them with every precaution, expecting and awaiting the complete destruction of them all in the morning.
The Gentiles thought that these Jews, because of their chains and bitter afflictions, had no help from anywhere, not even the slightest.
But they cried out, pleaded, and prayed without ceasing before God Almighty, the Lord of all powers, the merciful God and Father, with sobbing and many tears.
They asked him to rescue them from the evil intention and scheme being devised against them, to display his salvation openly among them, and to deliver them from the bitter death prepared for them.
Their plea for these things rose continually.
Hermon gave the merciless elephants wine mixed with frankincense to drink and made them drunk. At daybreak he came to the king’s courtyard to inform him of this.
But the Merciful One, the King of kings, cast sleep upon the king.

He slept deeply from evening until the ninth hour through the power of the One who rules over everything. He was delayed far beyond the time appointed for him to destroy them, and his proud and arrogant plan was thwarted.

When the Jews saw that they had escaped the hour appointed for them, they thanked and praised their holy God. Again they pleaded and begged the Merciful One to be fully reconciled to them and to show and make known the strength and help of his arm among the proud and arrogant nations.
For when the tenth hour was approaching, and his steward saw that all those invited by the king had come to the banquet, he approached and prodded the king in his side.
The king awoke only with difficulty. The steward informed him that it was time for the banquet and told him about everything that the king himself had planned to do.
When he heard this, he went to the drinking party and ordered everyone who had come for their banquet to recline opposite him.
He encouraged them to enjoy themselves, and when evening came, they lingered long over their drinking.
Amid much conversation, the king summoned Hermon in fierce anger and asked him why the Jews had escaped the day appointed for their destruction.
He answered him, “I prepared and made ready everything you commanded during the night.” His friends also testified and said that he had done so.

When he heard this, he did not humble himself from his proud and arrogant attitude, but boldly said to them, “Let them credit sleep with today’s kindness. But tomorrow, without any hindrance, prepare everything that was commanded, and make the elephants ready for the destruction and ruin of the Jews.”
When the king had given these orders, all his nobles went home rejoicing.
They could not sleep because of their anxious thoughts as they devised ways to destroy and ruin the Jews.
When the rooster crowed and dawn was near, Hermon equipped the elephants and came before the king’s courtyard.
The whole city was gathering to witness the outrage that was ready to befall the Jews at daybreak.

When the Jews saw that the hour appointed for their destruction was approaching, they wept many tears, stretched out their hands toward heaven, and cried out, begging the great and mighty God to help them quickly and urgently.
The king rose before sunrise and waited for his friends. Hermon approached and brought all the elephants before him, harnessed and armed according to the king’s command.

But when he saw it, he was astonished and amazed at the preparations for the outrage, for his mind was completely blinded concerning it. He asked them whether everything he had commanded had been done carefully.
This was God’s providence: he had put forgetfulness into his heart concerning what he had previously planned.
Hermon and all his friends approached and said to the king, “Everything you commanded is prepared and ready, both the elephants and the troops.”

When he heard these things from them, he was filled with great anger, because God’s mercies had so willed and brought his whole plan to nothing. He looked sternly at Hermon, insulted him with harsh words, and said to him:

“If they were your own people and your relatives, would you so mercilessly give the elephants drink and make them drunk, as you are doing against the Jews, my friends and loved ones, who are faithful in everything?
Were it not for our great mercy toward everyone, I would have destroyed your life in their place.”
Hermon was so terrified that he was only a little short of death. His complexion changed, and he was humbled from his proud attitude.
When his friends saw this, they too drew back in great fear and dismissed the people who were with them, each to his own place and work.
When the Jews heard the king’s words, they praised and thanked the Lord God, the King of kings, who had turned toward them and become their helper.
When the king had finished with these matters, he and all his friends went to the banquet.
He summoned Hermon and said to him angrily, “How often must someone give you orders concerning these wretches?
Go, prepare the elephants and make them ready for tomorrow, for the destruction and ruin of the Jews.”
His friends and relatives who were reclining with him, seeing his troubled mind and his wavering intentions, answered him:
“King, how long will you keep testing us? Three times now you have ordered their destruction, and then you turn around again and revoke your orders.
Because of this, the city too is gathering in crowds and is close to being entirely ruined by the daily turmoil.”

When the king heard this, he was filled with arrogance and pride, and his whole understanding was blinded. He forgot the help the Jews had received in the past and how his plan had already been thwarted three times. He swore an oath that would not be fulfilled, saying, “Tomorrow, before anything else, I will send these people down to Sheol, parents and children together, crushed in fury and trampled underfoot.

Then I will march against Judea again and quickly crush it and destroy it with sword and fire, making it level ground. Their temple, which they prevented me from entering, I will quickly burn with fire. I will destroy the place where they offer sacrifices and make it a wilderness forever.”

Then his friends and relatives left him joyfully, having heard him confirm by an oath that he would destroy them. They went and made preparations and gathered troops in the city's open spaces to keep watch over the Jews.

The man appointed over the elephants, following his orders, gave the elephants drink and made them drunk, greatly inflaming them with wine and frankincense. He brought them to the open space in the city.
A great crowd had gathered outside the city to witness the injustice. The man appointed over the elephants entered the king's courtyard and reported to him, stirring up his mind.

When he heard this, he was filled with fury, great anger, and wicked intentions. He took his entire army, together with the elephants and all his equipment, and went out. With a hard heart and a wicked eye, he wanted to look on and witness the death and suffering of those poor, miserable people.
When the elephants went out through the city gate, a great crowd followed them. When the Jews saw the great cloud of dust rising and heard the sound of the tremendous uproar,

they thought that the hour of their final end had come. Weeping and shedding many tears, they kissed one another, and each embraced his relative. Others, seeing the babies nursing, wept and sighed over them because the hour of their end had come.
Remembering the help and deliverance from heaven that they had received in the past, they all threw themselves to the ground and took the babies away from their mothers' breasts.
With sobbing and a great, mighty cry, they called out to the one whose power can accomplish everything he wills, asking him in his abundant mercy to help those who now stood at the gates of death.

Eleazar, a well-known man who was one of the foremost priests, was advanced in years and faultless in every aspect of his service in the fear of God. He instructed the elders of his people to pray and plead with the holy God. He himself also prayed, saying:
“King, mighty in dominion, Most High, who rules over all and governs your entire creation with mercy,

look upon and turn toward Abraham's descendants and the children of Jacob, your holy one—the holy portion you chose for yourself, your people in a foreign land, a poor people living as strangers, perishing needlessly through injustice, Father.

You drowned and destroyed Pharaoh, the mighty ruler of Egypt, in the depths of the sea, together with his powerful and exalted army. He had multiplied his chariots and had exalted himself, carried away by great pride and a tongue that spoke boastful things. But you made the light of mercy shine upon Israel's descendants.

You crushed and humbled Sennacherib, king of Assyria, Lord. He had exalted himself and boasted of his countless troops, who had conquered and seized many lands. He even exalted himself against your holy city and spoke blasphemous and arrogant words. You made your great and mighty dominion known to many nations.

You protected the three companions in Babylon within the fiery furnace. They had surrendered themselves to burning fire rather than serve empty and worthless things. You brought them out unharmed, without injury to so much as a hair, while the fiery flame burned their enemies.
You also brought Daniel out into the light without injury after he had been slandered and thrown into the lions' den for them to maul and destroy him.

And Jonah was thrown into the depths of the sea and swallowed by a fish. He wept and prayed before you from the fish's belly, and you heard his voice, preserved his life, and rescued him from the fish's belly. You showed all generations your power and greatness, Father.

And now we are here in disgrace and great distress. You are merciful and spread your wings over everyone. Look upon and turn quickly toward Israel's descendants, who are now being humiliated by wicked and unclean nations.
If our sins and offenses testify against us that we should die in this way, save us, Lord, from the hands of our enemies. Then discipline us and destroy us with your own hands, as you wish.
Do not let the foolish praise their empty idols over the destruction of those you love and say, “Even their God could not help them or save them.”

You are the Lord from whom all power and strength come, the one who has existed from eternity. Now look, Lord, and have mercy on us, on those who are perishing needlessly at the hands of wicked and foolish people.
But let your invincible power be revealed today, so that it may bring fear and trembling upon these nations, throw their hearts into confusion, and save the descendants of Israel.
For look, this multitude of children and their families asks you and implores you with tears and great weeping.

Let all the nations know that you are with us, Lord, and have not turned your face away from us. Rather, as you said, “Even when they were in the land of their enemies, I did not turn my eyes away from them,” so now also fulfill your promise to us, Lord.
When Eleazar finished his prayer, the king came with his entire army and the equipment he had with him to the place where the Jews were staying.
When the Jews saw this, they raised a great cry to heaven, so that the whole earth shook and all the king’s forces were terrified by the sound of their cry.

Then the Lord Almighty, great in glory and the God of truth, made his holy face shine and opened the gates of heaven. Two glorious and fearsome angels came down, visible to no one except the Jews alone.
They stood facing the enemies and filled their entire army and their camps with fear, trembling, and terror. They bound and restrained them so that they could not move.
They brought trembling and shuddering upon the king’s body, and he completely lost his lofty and arrogant resolve, which had been blazing with anger and fury.
The elephants turned against his forces and trampled, destroyed, and killed them.
The king’s anger turned to compassion, and he wept over everything he had devised and prepared to do.
For when he heard the sound of their cry and saw them all lying facedown as though awaiting destruction, he wept and became furious with his friends. He said to them,

“Your wickedness has gone beyond that of kings and tyrants! You plot against your own benefactor, seeking to take his authority away from him. Look, you see that my spirit is exhausted, yet you devise things that are harmful to the kingdom.
Who bound like this those who maintained friendship with us and guarded the fortresses of our land, and brought them here like animals?

Or who bound and subjected to harsh suffering those who, from the beginning and at all times, have lived peacefully with us, maintained friendship with us more than all the other nations, and stood against our enemies many times?
Undo, undo these unjust bonds, and send them home in peace! We devised evil and brought them here.

Release the children of the Almighty, the God of heaven, who has been with our ancestors from long ago and with us ourselves, who has protected our kingdom from every hardship and affliction and has always set our paths straight.”
When the king said these things, they were all released. They blessed and thanked God their Savior because they had been delivered from death.

After this, the king entered the city and ordered that wine and provisions be given to the Jews for seven days. He said that in the very place he had prepared for them to die and perish, they should hold a joyful feast celebrating their deliverance.

Then those who had previously been insulted and had come close to death—indeed, had even reached it—celebrated their deliverance with rejoicing instead of distress and bitter mourning. The place prepared for them to fall and be buried in, they divided into areas for reclining at the feast, and it was filled with celebration and joy.

They left behind distress and mourning and took up the hymns and psalms of their ancestors. With loud voices and shouts, they thanked and blessed God, who had worked wonders for them. They rejoiced and celebrated the sign of peace he had given them.
The king himself also held a great feast and invited many people. He continually gave thanks to the God of heaven, who had delivered him with great glory.

But those who had previously prepared for the destruction of the Jews and had joyfully registered their number so that they would become food for wild animals and birds, when they saw what was happening to them, groaned and became distressed and were clothed in shame. Their insolence and their anger, which had burned like fire, were extinguished, and they were left in shame and disgrace.
The Jews, however, as we said before, celebrated with feasting, rejoicing, and gladness, with psalms, hymns, and thanksgiving.

They agreed among themselves that wherever they lived, they would celebrate these days with joy and gladness, not for the sake of food and drink, but because of the deliverance God had brought about for them.
They approached the king and asked to be released and allowed to go home.
They had been registered from the twenty-fifth of the month until the fourth, forty days. For they had appointed three days, from the fifth until the seventh, in which to destroy them.
During those days the Lord, who rules over all, displayed the glory of his greatness and his mercy, and delivered them through a great miracle.
They all enjoyed what the king had given them until the fourteenth, on which day they had approached the king to ask to be sent away.
The king praised them and wrote the following letter for them to the governors in all the cities, expressing his great appreciation for them:
King Ptolemy Philometor, to all the governors in Egypt and all those who administer our affairs: peace and good health.
We ourselves, our children, and our affairs are all well, because the great God has put our affairs in order as we wished.

Some of our friends and those who were very closely associated with us, because of their hatred of the Jews, persuaded us to gather all the Jews under our authority, torture and destroy them, and torment them with every kind of affliction.
They said that these people would not allow our kingdom to enjoy peace and tranquility, because of the hostility they themselves bore toward all the Jews and their hatred of them.

They bound them and brought them here as though they were wicked and condemned criminals, without trial or investigation. They wanted to kill and destroy them all together, with wickedness, rage, and a tyranny with which they clothed themselves even more than the Scythians.

But we were distressed by these things and became very angry. In keeping with the compassion and gentleness we have toward everyone, we barely managed to rescue them from death and grant them their lives. We learned with certainty that God is the helper of the Jews and fights for them as a father fights for his children.
Considering their friendship and peaceful relations with us and our ancestors, we released them, free from every charge whatsoever.
We have ordered that whatever was taken from each of them be returned to him, and that no one wrong them even slightly or reproach them for anything that happened to them.

You should know that if we scheme against them and do them any harm, or trouble them in any way, we are acting not against a human being but against the Most High God, who rules over every power. For he is the avenger of these people, and no one can flee or escape from him. Farewell.
When they received the letter, they did not wish to depart immediately. Instead, they asked the king that those Jews who had voluntarily turned aside and departed from the holy God and his law,
because of the greed of their bellies, should receive the punishment and judgment they deserved, since they had not proved faithful even in the king’s affairs.

When he heard that they were speaking truthfully, he accepted their request, praised them, and gave them authority to kill and destroy all the apostates and transgressors of the law under the authority of his kingdom, wherever they wished, at their own discretion.
Then the priests and the people praised the king as was fitting, raised their voices in a song of praise to him, and went out rejoicing.
As they traveled along the road, they put every apostate who fell into their hands to a cruel and public death.
On that day they killed three hundred men and celebrated with great joy, and they killed all the defiled people.

Those whose helper God had been even in the face of death, and whom he had completely delivered from every affliction, left the city crowned with all kinds of fragrant flowers. With joy and gladness they gave thanks and praised the God of their ancestors with magnificent songs of praise, for he is Israel’s deliverer forever.
When they came to Ptolemais, which is called Rose-Crowned because of the beauty of its setting, all the city’s inhabitants came out together and greeted them peacefully. They stayed there seven days
and enjoyed themselves greatly, for the king had ordered that they be supplied with provisions at his expense until each of them had reached home safely.
They celebrated these days with fitting songs of praise and thanksgiving, and there too they established that they would celebrate those days with joy and gladness throughout their lives.

At the place where they had camped, they set up a pillar and built a house of prayer there. They departed joyfully, rejoicing and celebrating, each to his own country and city, by sea, by land, and by the rivers.
By the king’s command, they were exalted and raised above their enemies.
They recovered everything that had been plundered from them, and no one dared to wrong them even a little, because of the great deliverance that the great and mighty God had accomplished for them.
And blessed is the Savior of Israel forever and ever.
